screens.title: Configuring Postfix as an SMTP Server
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to turn a Linux host into a properly configured SMTP server using Postfix. We'll focus on the authoritative configuration file, /etc/postfix/main. cf, and the key parameters that determine server identity, network listening, trusted clients, and access control. You will see concrete examples of myhostname and mydomain settings, how to choose inet_interfaces and inet_protocols for the interfaces you want Postfix to bind, and how mynetworks and smtpd_recipient_restrictions work together to prevent your server becoming an open relay. We'll also cover the practical DNS requirements: an MX record for your domain that points to your mail hostname, and an A record for that hostname mapping to your public IP. Finally, you'll learn simple verification and troubleshooting steps, including reloading Postfix after changes, checking postconf output, sending test mail from trusted and untrusted clients, and inspecting logs and dig results. By the end of this chapter you'll understand both the correct configuration options and the common misconfigurations that lead to rejected mail or blacklisting. Consider how each parameter you edit affects who can send, who can receive, and how other mail servers find you.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this first objectives screen we'll make clear the practical configuration skills you'll gain. First, you'll be able to edit /etc/postfix/main. cf to configure essential Postfix parameters so SMTP works for your domain. That includes setting myhostname and mydomain correctly so your server identifies itself with a resolvable name. Second, you'll implement sender and recipient restrictions to prevent unauthorized relaying. This teaches you to use mynetworks and smtpd_recipient_restrictions so only trusted clients or authenticated users may relay. Third, you'll understand how DNS influences mail delivery: MX records point to your mail host and that host must have an A record mapping to its IP. Fourth, you'll configure which network interfaces and IP protocols Postfix listens on with inet_interfaces and inet_protocols so your server accepts connections where you expect them. Each objective is tied to concrete configuration lines and verification commands so you can test and confirm behavior in a lab. By the end you'll not only change settings but also validate that mail flows and that your server is not open to abuse.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen lists the practical validation and troubleshooting abilities you'll gain. First, you'll identify and mitigate common misconfigurations that cause mail rejection or security issues, such as overly permissive mynetworks or missing MX records. Second, you'll reliably reload Postfix after changing main. cf so the running daemon picks up updates; reloading is required because Postfix does not automatically re-read the file. Third, you'll know how to test internal versus external relay behavior by sending mail from a trusted client inside mynetworks and from an untrusted client outside it, and interpreting 'Relay access denied' messages. Fourth, you will use postconf -n, journalctl -u postfix or /var/log/maillog along with dig MX and dig A to verify configuration and DNS. These skills let you not only set configuration but also prove it works in a lab or production environment and quickly find the cause when mail fails to deliver.

screens.title: Server Identity: myhostname and mydomain
screens.narratorSegment: A clear server identity is the foundation of correct SMTP interactions. The myhostname parameter defines the fully qualified domain name Postfix uses when presenting itself to other mail servers. This name must resolve in DNS with an A record that points to the server's public IP; otherwise remote MTAs may mark mail as suspicious or fail to connect. Complementing myhostname is mydomain, which tells Postfix the local internet domain for mail delivery decisions. For example, setting myhostname to mail. example. com and mydomain to example. com ensures that outgoing clients see mail. example. com as the server identity while local deliveries map to example. com. A common misconception is thinking the machine's kernel hostname is sufficient; Postfix uses the explicit myhostname value for SMTP transactions, and the absence or misconfiguration of this parameter can mean HELO/EHLO names don't match DNS, causing reputation or delivery problems. In practice, update /etc/postfix/main. cf with these lines and verify with postconf -n to confirm the effective settings. Also check that dig A mail. example. com returns the server IP and that MX for example. com points to mail. example. com. As a takeaway, always ensure the names you configure in Postfix have matching DNS records; a mismatch is a frequent root cause of rejected connections or deliverability issues. What DNS check will you run first after changing myhostname?

keyIdea.title: Identity matters
keyIdea.text: Set myhostname and mydomain to resolvable names with matching DNS; this prevents HELO mismatches and improves deliverability.

content.html:
Core Concept

Server Identity

myhostname sets the FQDN Postfix advertises. mydomain defines the local internet domain used for local delivery decisions.

# /etc/postfix/main.cf myhostname = mail.example.com mydomain = example.com
Concrete example
If myhostname = mail.example.com and DNS has an A record for that name, other MTAs can resolve and connect to your server.
Common misconception
Using only the system hostname or an internal name without a public A record will break remote delivery and can look suspicious to receiving servers.
Verification steps
postconf -n
# verify DNS
dig A mail.example.com
dig MX example.com
Why it matters
  • HELO/EHLO name should match a resolvable A record to avoid rejections.
  • mydomain controls which destinations are considered local for delivery.
  • Misconfigured identity can cause reputation and routing issues.
Key Takeaway

Always configure myhostname to an FQDN that has an A record; set mydomain to the domain you serve so local delivery rules align with DNS.

screens.title: Binding Postfix: inet_interfaces and inet_protocols
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing which network interfaces and IP protocols Postfix listens on determines who can reach your SMTP service. The inet_interfaces parameter controls which addresses Postfix binds to. A common lab setting is inet_interfaces = all so Postfix listens on every available interface, but in production it's safer to list specific addresses especially if the host has multiple NICs or is behind NAT. For example, inet_interfaces = $myhostname, localhost, 192.168.1.100 binds to those named addresses only. A related parameter, inet_protocols, restricts IP versions: values include all, ipv4, or ipv6. If your environment is IPv4-only, set inet_protocols = ipv4 to avoid unexpected IPv6 behavior. A frequent misconception is assuming firewall rules alone are enough: while firewalls help, binding Postfix only where needed reduces exposure and accidental acceptance of mail on unintended networks. After changing these settings, reload Postfix and then check with netstat or ss to confirm listening sockets match your intent. As a concrete example, bind only loopback and a private interface for an internal relay, or all interfaces for an internet-facing server with proper firewalling. The takeaway is to align inet_interfaces and inet_protocols with your network topology and security posture; think deliberately about which addresses should accept SMTP traffic.

keyIdea.title: Bind deliberately
keyIdea.text: Use inet_interfaces and inet_protocols to limit the network surfaces Postfix listens on; prefer explicit addresses in multi-homed or NAT environments.

content.html:
Process Flow

Bind Postfix to specific interfaces

Decide which IPs and protocols should accept SMTP connections and reflect that in main.cf.

# examples inet_interfaces = all inet_interfaces = $myhostname, localhost, 192.168.1.100 inet_protocols = all inet_protocols = ipv4
Concrete example
For an internal relay set inet_interfaces to localhost and the internal IP so public networks can't connect directly.
Verification
# reload after edit
sudo systemctl reload postfix
# confirm listening sockets
ss -ltnp | grep :25
Misconception
Relying only on a firewall while leaving inet_interfaces = all increases the risk of accidental exposure if firewall rules change. Bind intentionally where possible.
Key Takeaway

Match inet_interfaces and inet_protocols to your topology; explicit bindings reduce accidental exposure and simplify firewall rules.

screens.title: mynetworks: Trusted clients versus open relay
screens.narratorSegment: The mynetworks parameter lists ranges and hosts that Postfix treats as trusted. Clients in mynetworks are allowed to relay mail to arbitrary destinations, which is necessary for internal services or users, but dangerous if defined too broadly. An open relay occurs when mynetworks includes large public ranges or a wildcard, allowing spammers to send mail through your server. A typical safe value includes loopback and your internal subnets, for example 127.0.0.0/8 [::1]/128 192.168.1.0/24. If you mistakenly leave out an internal client from mynetworks, that client cannot relay and will see 'Relay access denied'. Conversely, adding 0.0.0.0/0 or a broad public block inadvertently permits anyone to use your host to send mail. When configuring mynetworks, think in terms of minimal trust: include only the specific subnets and hosts that legitimately need to relay. Use CIDR notation to be precise. After changes, reload Postfix and test by sending mail from a client within the listed subnet and from one outside it to observe the contrasted behavior. That contrast — permitted internal relay versus rejected external attempt — is central to preventing abuse while supporting legitimate traffic. Which IP ranges should you include and why?

keyIdea.title: Trust explicitly
keyIdea.text: mynetworks must list only trusted IP ranges; too broad a value creates an open relay, too narrow blocks legitimate internal senders.

content.html:
Comparison

Trusted vs Untrusted

Trusted (allowed relay)
127.0.0.0/8 [::1]/128 192.168.1.0/24 — clients here may relay to any destination.
Untrusted (blocked relay)
Any client not listed in mynetworks will be subject to recipient restrictions and typically rejected for external destinations.
# /etc/postfix/main.cf mynetworks = 127.0.0.0/8 [::1]/128 192.168.1.0/24
Pitfall example
Adding an overly broad range such as 0.0.0.0/0 results in an open relay and immediate abuse, often ending in blacklisting. Always prefer the narrowest range that meets operational needs.
Testing strategy
# internal test
echo "Test" | mail -s "Internal Relay Test" external@example.com
# external test should be blocked from untrusted host
Pro Tip

When in doubt, remove a range and re-add it narrowly after verifying which hosts need relay access.

screens.title: mydestination and Local Delivery
screens.narratorSegment: The mydestination parameter lists domains for which this Postfix instance is the final destination. Mail addressed to domains included in mydestination is delivered locally rather than relayed onward. A typical setting includes the mail hostname, localhost forms, and the domain itself, for example mydestination = $myhostname, localhost.$mydomain, localhost, $mydomain. This tells Postfix to accept mail for mail. example. com and example. com and to deliver it to local mailboxes. A common mistake is omitting the domain you intend to host; if example. com is not in mydestination, Postfix will consider it non-local and may reject or attempt to relay messages depending on relay domains and ACLs. Conversely, adding domains unintentionally can cause Postfix to accept mail for domains you don't serve, which could be a security or routing error. After editing main. cf, reload Postfix and test by sending mail to local users; check the mail queue and logs for delivery. As a concrete example, if you're serving example. com and mail. example. com on the same machine, include both entries in mydestination so the server will accept and deliver messages for them.

keyIdea.title: Local domains
keyIdea.text: mydestination lists domains treated as local by Postfix; include only domains you are authoritative for to ensure correct local delivery.

content.html:
Definition

What mydestination does

It lists the domains Postfix should accept and deliver locally instead of relaying elsewhere.

# example mydestination = $myhostname, localhost.$mydomain, localhost, $mydomain
Concrete example
If you host example.com, include it in mydestination so mail for user@example.com is delivered locally.
Misconfiguration
Omitting your domain will cause Postfix to treat local mail as non-local and trigger relay checks or rejection.
Verification
Send a message to a local user and watch the mail log to confirm local delivery rather than relay attempts.
# send a local test
echo "Local delivery test" | mail -s "Local Test" localuser
# check logs
journalctl -u postfix --since "5 minutes ago"
Key Takeaway

Only include domains you should accept mail for in mydestination to avoid accidental acceptance or rejection of mail.

screens.title: smtpd_recipient_restrictions and ACL order
screens.narratorSegment: Postfix evaluates recipient-based access controls in the order they appear in smtpd_recipient_restrictions. A safe, minimal sequence is permit_mynetworks, permit_sasl_authenticated, reject_unauth_destination. permit_mynetworks grants relay to clients in the mynetworks list. permit_sasl_authenticated allows authenticated users to relay regardless of IP. reject_unauth_destination is the crucial protective rule that rejects attempts to send mail to non-local domains unless the sender is trusted or authenticated. The order matters: if reject_unauth_destination appeared before permit_mynetworks, trusted clients might be rejected. A concrete configuration looks like smtpd_recipient_restrictions = permit_mynetworks permit_sasl_authenticated reject_unauth_destination. A common misconception is thinking these are independent toggles; they are evaluated sequentially, and an allow rule earlier short-circuits later checks. When you test, try sending an external address from a host in mynetworks and from an unauthenticated external host: one should succeed, the other should be rejected with 'Relay access denied'. Keep in mind this list can include finer-grained checks, but the three-rule pattern prevents open relay while supporting trusted internal and authenticated clients. Ask yourself whether your sequence could inadvertently allow unwanted relays. smtpd_recipient_restrictions and ACL order means place permit rules before reject_unauth_destination so trusted clients and authenticated users are allowed while others are rejected.. In practical terms, rule order matters: permit_mynetworks, permit_sasl_authenticated, reject_unauth_destination. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow

Recipient Restrictions

A simple, effective sequence prevents open relay while allowing trusted traffic.

# /etc/postfix/main.cf smtpd_recipient_restrictions = permit_mynetworks permit_sasl_authenticated reject_unauth_destination
Why reject_unauth_destination
It blocks any recipient not listed in mydestination, relay_domains, or virtual_alias_domains unless the sender is trusted or authenticated.
Order matters
An allow rule placed after a reject can be skipped. Always place permit rules first for expected behavior.
Concrete test
From a trusted client in mynetworks send mail to external recipient; from an untrusted host repeat the test and observe rejection.
# internal test
echo "Test" | mail -s "Internal" user@example.com
# external test should show 'Relay access denied' in logs
Key Takeaway

Build recipient restrictions in a clear order: allow trusted networks and authenticated users first, then reject unauthorised destinations.

screens.title: Hands-on: Editing main.cf and reloading Postfix
screens.narratorSegment: Making changes to main. cf is straightforward but requires a reload to take effect. After editing /etc/postfix/main. cf, run sudo systemctl reload postfix to have Postfix re-read the file without interrupting in-flight mail. Use postconf -n to display the active non-default settings and confirm your edits are recognized. A typical workflow is to open main. cf, modify myhostname, mydomain, inet_interfaces, and mynetworks as needed, then save and reload. If postconf -n still shows old values, it usually means you forgot to reload. A useful concrete command set is: edit main. cf, then run sudo systemctl reload postfix followed by postconf -n. Check logs with journalctl -u postfix or /var/log/maillog to see whether the daemon logged configuration reload success or errors. A common misconception is that restart is always required; reload is sufficient for most main. cf updates and is less disruptive. However, if a setting fails to apply or you see configuration parsing errors, Postfix will log the problem; inspect those messages and correct main. cf, then reload again. As a takeaway, always verify with postconf -n and logs after a reload so you are confident the running service reflects your intended configuration.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Edit, Reload, Verify

# edit /etc/postfix/main.cf sudo nano /etc/postfix/main.cf # then reload sudo systemctl reload postfix # check settings postconf -n
Concrete example
Change myhostname to mail.example.com, save, run systemctl reload postfix, and confirm postconf -n shows the new name.
Troubleshooting tips
  • If postconf -n shows the old value, reload Postfix; the service does not auto-reload.
  • Check journalctl -u postfix for parse errors or warnings after reload.
  • Use postconf -n to see only non-default values you changed.
Key Takeaway

Follow edit → reload → verify. postconf -n and the service logs are your primary verification tools after a configuration change.

screens.title: DNS Requirements: MX and A Records
screens.narratorSegment: DNS is essential to mail delivery. An MX record for your domain points mail-sending MTAs to the hostname responsible for receiving mail. That MX hostname must have an A record mapping to an IPv4 address that remote servers can connect to. For example, example. com should have an MX record such as mail. example. com, and mail. example. com must have an A record that resolves to the server's public IP. Without these records, sending MTAs won't know where to send mail for your domain, and delivery will fail. The chapter demonstrates using dig to verify records: dig MX example. com and dig A mail. example. com. A misconception is assuming an A record for the naked domain suffices for mail; the MX record explicitly directs mail traffic and should be set correctly. After updating DNS, allow time for propagation and then re-run dig to confirm. Note that missing or mispointed records commonly result in 'Host not found' or connection errors in Postfix logs. As a concrete step, create the MX and A records at your DNS provider, then test with dig and attempt a delivery; use the logs to correlate DNS resolution and connection attempts. The key insight is that DNS must direct mail traffic to an IP that your Postfix instance actually listens on and accepts connections from.

keyIdea.title: DNS alignment
keyIdea.text: An MX record must point to a hostname with a matching A record to allow other MTAs to locate and connect to your Postfix server.

content.html:
Definition

MX and A records for mail

Ensure your domain's MX points to your mail hostname and that hostname has an A record to your server IP.

# verify DNS dig MX example.com dig A mail.example.com
Concrete example
If MX for example.com is mail.example.com but mail.example.com has no A record, remote MTAs cannot connect to deliver mail.
Common errors
  • MX pointing to a name without an A record causes 'Host not found' or connection failures.
  • Pointing an MX to a hostname that resolves to a private IP will fail for internet senders.
  • Remember to allow DNS propagation before testing externally.
Key Takeaway

Confirm MX and A records with dig and ensure the A record points to the public IP where Postfix listens for SMTP connections.

screens.title: Testing: Internal and External Relay Attempts
screens.narratorSegment: Testing your Postfix configuration is the final step to ensure correctness and security. The hands-on activity in the source walks you through changing main. cf, reloading Postfix, and performing two tests: an internal relay test from a client inside mynetworks, and an external relay attempt from a client outside that range. For the internal test, send an email from a host within the trusted network and expect successful delivery to an external address like your personal inbox. On the server, inspect /var/log/maillog or journalctl -u postfix to confirm the message was accepted and handed off. For the external test, either use a machine not listed in mynetworks or temporarily remove the client's IP from mynetworks and reload Postfix; when that host attempts to send to an external recipient, Postfix should reject with 'Relay access denied' and the logs should show the rejection. This contrast verifies that permit_mynetworks and reject_unauth_destination are working together. A common pitfall is forgetting to reload after modifying mynetworks, which will leave the behavior unchanged. As a final question, after a successful internal test and a rejected external test, what log entry will prove the relay was explicitly denied? Look for 'relay access denied' as the proof.

keyIdea.title: Test contrast
keyIdea.text: Use both an internal and external send attempt to confirm that trusted clients can relay and untrusted clients are rejected.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Internal vs External Tests

# internal client (trusted) echo "Test email from internal client." | mail -s "Internal Relay Test" your_personal_email@gmail.com # external client (untrusted) echo "Test email from external client." | mail -s "External Relay Test" your_personal_email@gmail.com
Expected outcome
Internal test succeeds; external test fails with 'Relay access denied' visible in logs.
Verification commands
# logs
journalctl -u postfix --since "10 minutes ago"
# or
tail -f /var/log/maillog
Common Mistake

Forgetting to reload Postfix after editing mynetworks leaves behavior unchanged; always reload and re-test.

screens.title: Common Errors and Log Messages
screens.narratorSegment: Reading logs is essential to diagnose mail flow problems. Two common error messages are 'Relay access denied' and 'Host not found'. 'Relay access denied' typically indicates the client attempting to send was not in mynetworks and was not authenticated, so reject_unauth_destination blocked the relay. 'Host not found' is often a DNS issue where the MX or A record is missing or points to a name that doesn't resolve. When you see a delivery failure, correlate the timestamp with the sending attempt and examine the surrounding log lines to find the actionable cause—missing DNS, wrong mydestination, or binding issues on the listening interface. For example, if the logs show connection attempts but then a name resolution failure, verify the MX and A records with dig. If the server refuses to accept a message from an internal host, check mynetworks contents and whether the host's IP is included. Use postconf -n to confirm what Postfix believes its configuration is after a reload. A misconception is to assume mail failures are always network problems; many are configuration errors in main. cf. As a practical habit, after every test failure check the logs first, then postconf -n, and finally DNS with dig. That three-step routine quickly isolates whether the issue is configuration, DNS, or network reachability.

keyIdea.title: Logs first
keyIdea.text: Use logs to identify whether failures are due to relay denials, DNS resolution, or binding errors; follow logs → postconf → dig to isolate causes.

content.html:
Troubleshooting

Interpreting common log messages

Start with the log entry and timestamp, then check configuration and DNS to determine the root cause.
# common messages Relay access denied -> client not trusted or authenticated Host not found -> MX or A record missing or incorrect status=deferred -> delivery delayed or DNS/recipient resolution failed
Diagnostic routine
  1. Check logs for the error line and nearby context.
  2. Confirm current Postfix settings with postconf -n.
  3. Verify DNS with dig MX and dig A for hostnames involved.
Key Takeaway

Logs provide the fastest path to the cause: match times, inspect configuration, then verify DNS to find why mail was rejected or deferred.

First, ensure main. cf contains the intended myhostname and mydomain, confirm inet_interfaces and inet_protocols align with your topology, and verify mydestination lists the domains you own. Next, check mynetworks for a minimal trusted set and confirm smtpd_recipient_restrictions includes permit_mynetworks, permit_sasl_authenticated, and reject_unauth_destination. Reload Postfix and run postconf -n to validate the active configuration. Perform an internal send from a trusted client and an external send from an untrusted client; the internal should succeed and the external should produce 'Relay access denied'. Use journalctl or /var/log/maillog and dig MX/A to verify DNS and delivery. The chapter's assessment asks whether an internal client IP will be allowed to relay when mynetworks contains only 127.0.0.0/8; the correct answer is no, because the internal client is not in the trusted set. This demonstrates how mynetworks controls relay permissions. content.html:
Assessment & Lab

Final checklist

  • Set myhostname and mydomain and verify with postconf -n.
  • Configure inet_interfaces and inet_protocols to match your network plan.
  • Define a minimal mynetworks and set smtpd_recipient_restrictions appropriately.
  • Ensure MX and A records point to your mail host and verify using dig.
  • Reload Postfix, run internal and external relay tests, and inspect logs.
Assessment question
If mynetworks = 127.0.0.0/8 and an internal client 192.168.1.50 tries to send mail to externaluser@anotherdomain.com, will it relay?
Answer: No. 192.168.1.50 is not in mynetworks, so permit_mynetworks won't apply and reject_unauth_destination will block relay.
Key Takeaway

Use the assessment to confirm you understand how mynetworks and recipient restrictions interact; test to prove your conclusion.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the compact concepts you should remember from configuring Postfix as an SMTP server. First, myhostname and mydomain establish the server's identity; they must match DNS so HELO/EHLO names are resolvable. Second, inet_interfaces and inet_protocols determine where Postfix listens; prefer explicit bindings for multi-homed or NAT environments to reduce exposure. Third, mynetworks defines trusted networks that may relay; keep this list narrow to avoid open relay. Each of these concepts interacts: a correct identity without proper DNS is useless, binding to the wrong interface prevents delivery, and an overbroad mynetworks creates security problems. Carry these three core ideas into your configurations and tests to keep mail flowing securely and predictably. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to turn a Linux host into a properly configured SMTP server using Postfix. We'll focus on the authoritative configuration file, /etc/postfix/main. cf, and the key parameters that determine server identity, network listening, trusted clients, and access control. You will see concrete examples of myhostname and mydomain settings, how to choose inet_interfaces and inet_protocols for the interfaces you want Postfix to bind, and how mynetworks and smtpd_recipient_restrictions work together to prevent your server becoming an open relay. We'll also cover the practical DNS requirements: an MX record for your domain that points to your mail hostname, and an A record for that hostname mapping to your public IP. Finally, you'll learn simple verification and troubleshooting steps, including reloading Postfix after changes, checking postconf output, sending test mail from trusted and untrusted clients, and inspecting logs and dig results. By the end of this chapter you'll understand both the correct configuration options and the common misconfigurations that lead to rejected mail or blacklisting. Consider how each parameter you edit affects who can send, who can receive, and how other mail servers find you.

In this first objectives screen we'll make clear the practical configuration skills you'll gain. First, you'll be able to edit /etc/postfix/main. cf to configure essential Postfix parameters so SMTP works for your domain. That includes setting myhostname and mydomain correctly so your server identifies itself with a resolvable name. Second, you'll implement sender and recipient restrictions to prevent unauthorized relaying. This teaches you to use mynetworks and smtpd_recipient_restrictions so only trusted clients or authenticated users may relay. Third, you'll understand how DNS influences mail delivery: MX records point to your mail host and that host must have an A record mapping to its IP. Fourth, you'll configure which network interfaces and IP protocols Postfix listens on with inet_interfaces and inet_protocols so your server accepts connections where you expect them. Each objective is tied to concrete configuration lines and verification commands so you can test and confirm behavior in a lab. By the end you'll not only change settings but also validate that mail flows and that your server is not open to abuse.

This second objectives screen lists the practical validation and troubleshooting abilities you'll gain. First, you'll identify and mitigate common misconfigurations that cause mail rejection or security issues, such as overly permissive mynetworks or missing MX records. Second, you'll reliably reload Postfix after changing main. cf so the running daemon picks up updates; reloading is required because Postfix does not automatically re-read the file. Third, you'll know how to test internal versus external relay behavior by sending mail from a trusted client inside mynetworks and from an untrusted client outside it, and interpreting 'Relay access denied' messages. Fourth, you will use postconf -n, journalctl -u postfix or /var/log/maillog along with dig MX and dig A to verify configuration and DNS. These skills let you not only set configuration but also prove it works in a lab or production environment and quickly find the cause when mail fails to deliver.

A clear server identity is the foundation of correct SMTP interactions. The myhostname parameter defines the fully qualified domain name Postfix uses when presenting itself to other mail servers. This name must resolve in DNS with an A record that points to the server's public IP; otherwise remote MTAs may mark mail as suspicious or fail to connect. Complementing myhostname is mydomain, which tells Postfix the local internet domain for mail delivery decisions. For example, setting myhostname to mail. example. com and mydomain to example. com ensures that outgoing clients see mail. example. com as the server identity while local deliveries map to example. com. A common misconception is thinking the machine's kernel hostname is sufficient; Postfix uses the explicit myhostname value for SMTP transactions, and the absence or misconfiguration of this parameter can mean HELO/EHLO names don't match DNS, causing reputation or delivery problems. In practice, update /etc/postfix/main. cf with these lines and verify with postconf -n to confirm the effective settings. Also check that dig A mail. example. com returns the server IP and that MX for example. com points to mail. example. com. As a takeaway, always ensure the names you configure in Postfix have matching DNS records; a mismatch is a frequent root cause of rejected connections or deliverability issues. What DNS check will you run first after changing myhostname?

Choosing which network interfaces and IP protocols Postfix listens on determines who can reach your SMTP service. The inet_interfaces parameter controls which addresses Postfix binds to. A common lab setting is inet_interfaces = all so Postfix listens on every available interface, but in production it's safer to list specific addresses especially if the host has multiple NICs or is behind NAT. For example, inet_interfaces = $myhostname, localhost, 192.168.1.100 binds to those named addresses only. A related parameter, inet_protocols, restricts IP versions: values include all, ipv4, or ipv6. If your environment is IPv4-only, set inet_protocols = ipv4 to avoid unexpected IPv6 behavior. A frequent misconception is assuming firewall rules alone are enough: while firewalls help, binding Postfix only where needed reduces exposure and accidental acceptance of mail on unintended networks. After changing these settings, reload Postfix and then check with netstat or ss to confirm listening sockets match your intent. As a concrete example, bind only loopback and a private interface for an internal relay, or all interfaces for an internet-facing server with proper firewalling. The takeaway is to align inet_interfaces and inet_protocols with your network topology and security posture; think deliberately about which addresses should accept SMTP traffic.

The mynetworks parameter lists ranges and hosts that Postfix treats as trusted. Clients in mynetworks are allowed to relay mail to arbitrary destinations, which is necessary for internal services or users, but dangerous if defined too broadly. An open relay occurs when mynetworks includes large public ranges or a wildcard, allowing spammers to send mail through your server. A typical safe value includes loopback and your internal subnets, for example 127.0.0.0/8 [::1]/128 192.168.1.0/24. If you mistakenly leave out an internal client from mynetworks, that client cannot relay and will see 'Relay access denied'. Conversely, adding 0.0.0.0/0 or a broad public block inadvertently permits anyone to use your host to send mail. When configuring mynetworks, think in terms of minimal trust: include only the specific subnets and hosts that legitimately need to relay. Use CIDR notation to be precise. After changes, reload Postfix and test by sending mail from a client within the listed subnet and from one outside it to observe the contrasted behavior. That contrast — permitted internal relay versus rejected external attempt — is central to preventing abuse while supporting legitimate traffic. Which IP ranges should you include and why?

The mydestination parameter lists domains for which this Postfix instance is the final destination. Mail addressed to domains included in mydestination is delivered locally rather than relayed onward. A typical setting includes the mail hostname, localhost forms, and the domain itself, for example mydestination = $myhostname, localhost.$mydomain, localhost, $mydomain. This tells Postfix to accept mail for mail. example. com and example. com and to deliver it to local mailboxes. A common mistake is omitting the domain you intend to host; if example. com is not in mydestination, Postfix will consider it non-local and may reject or attempt to relay messages depending on relay domains and ACLs. Conversely, adding domains unintentionally can cause Postfix to accept mail for domains you don't serve, which could be a security or routing error. After editing main. cf, reload Postfix and test by sending mail to local users; check the mail queue and logs for delivery. As a concrete example, if you're serving example. com and mail. example. com on the same machine, include both entries in mydestination so the server will accept and deliver messages for them.

Postfix evaluates recipient-based access controls in the order they appear in smtpd_recipient_restrictions. A safe, minimal sequence is permit_mynetworks, permit_sasl_authenticated, reject_unauth_destination. permit_mynetworks grants relay to clients in the mynetworks list. permit_sasl_authenticated allows authenticated users to relay regardless of IP. reject_unauth_destination is the crucial protective rule that rejects attempts to send mail to non-local domains unless the sender is trusted or authenticated. The order matters: if reject_unauth_destination appeared before permit_mynetworks, trusted clients might be rejected. A concrete configuration looks like smtpd_recipient_restrictions = permit_mynetworks permit_sasl_authenticated reject_unauth_destination. A common misconception is thinking these are independent toggles; they are evaluated sequentially, and an allow rule earlier short-circuits later checks. When you test, try sending an external address from a host in mynetworks and from an unauthenticated external host: one should succeed, the other should be rejected with 'Relay access denied'. Keep in mind this list can include finer-grained checks, but the three-rule pattern prevents open relay while supporting trusted internal and authenticated clients. Ask yourself whether your sequence could inadvertently allow unwanted relays. smtpd_recipient_restrictions and ACL order means place permit rules before reject_unauth_destination so trusted clients and authenticated users are allowed while others are rejected.. In practical terms, rule order matters: permit_mynetworks, permit_sasl_authenticated, reject_unauth_destination. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Making changes to main. cf is straightforward but requires a reload to take effect. After editing /etc/postfix/main. cf, run sudo systemctl reload postfix to have Postfix re-read the file without interrupting in-flight mail. Use postconf -n to display the active non-default settings and confirm your edits are recognized. A typical workflow is to open main. cf, modify myhostname, mydomain, inet_interfaces, and mynetworks as needed, then save and reload. If postconf -n still shows old values, it usually means you forgot to reload. A useful concrete command set is: edit main. cf, then run sudo systemctl reload postfix followed by postconf -n. Check logs with journalctl -u postfix or /var/log/maillog to see whether the daemon logged configuration reload success or errors. A common misconception is that restart is always required; reload is sufficient for most main. cf updates and is less disruptive. However, if a setting fails to apply or you see configuration parsing errors, Postfix will log the problem; inspect those messages and correct main. cf, then reload again. As a takeaway, always verify with postconf -n and logs after a reload so you are confident the running service reflects your intended configuration.

DNS is essential to mail delivery. An MX record for your domain points mail-sending MTAs to the hostname responsible for receiving mail. That MX hostname must have an A record mapping to an IPv4 address that remote servers can connect to. For example, example. com should have an MX record such as mail. example. com, and mail. example. com must have an A record that resolves to the server's public IP. Without these records, sending MTAs won't know where to send mail for your domain, and delivery will fail. Testing your Postfix configuration is the final step to ensure correctness and security. The hands-on activity in the source walks you through changing main. cf, reloading Postfix, and performing two tests: an internal relay test from a client inside mynetworks, and an external relay attempt from a client outside that range. For the internal test, send an email from a host within the trusted network and expect successful delivery to an external address like your personal inbox. On the server, inspect /var/log/maillog or journalctl -u postfix to confirm the message was accepted and handed off. For the external test, either use a machine not listed in mynetworks or temporarily remove the client's IP from mynetworks and reload Postfix; when that host attempts to send to an external recipient, Postfix should reject with 'Relay access denied' and the logs should show the rejection. This contrast verifies that permit_mynetworks and reject_unauth_destination are working together. A common pitfall is forgetting to reload after modifying mynetworks, which will leave the behavior unchanged. As a final question, after a successful internal test and a rejected external test, what log entry will prove the relay was explicitly denied? Look for 'relay access denied' as the proof.

Reading logs is essential to diagnose mail flow problems. Two common error messages are 'Relay access denied' and 'Host not found'. 'Relay access denied' typically indicates the client attempting to send was not in mynetworks and was not authenticated, so reject_unauth_destination blocked the relay. 'Host not found' is often a DNS issue where the MX or A record is missing or points to a name that doesn't resolve. When you see a delivery failure, correlate the timestamp with the sending attempt and examine the surrounding log lines to find the actionable cause—missing DNS, wrong mydestination, or binding issues on the listening interface. For example, if the logs show connection attempts but then a name resolution failure, verify the MX and A records with dig. If the server refuses to accept a message from an internal host, check mynetworks contents and whether the host's IP is included. Use postconf -n to confirm what Postfix believes its configuration is after a reload. A misconception is to assume mail failures are always network problems; many are configuration errors in main. cf. As a practical habit, after every test failure check the logs first, then postconf -n, and finally DNS with dig. That three-step routine quickly isolates whether the issue is configuration, DNS, or network reachability.

These are the compact concepts you should remember from configuring Postfix as an SMTP server. First, myhostname and mydomain establish the server's identity; they must match DNS so HELO/EHLO names are resolvable. Second, inet_interfaces and inet_protocols determine where Postfix listens; prefer explicit bindings for multi-homed or NAT environments to reduce exposure. Third, mynetworks defines trusted networks that may relay; keep this list narrow to avoid open relay. Each of these concepts interacts: a correct identity without proper DNS is useless, binding to the wrong interface prevents delivery, and an overbroad mynetworks creates security problems. Carry these three core ideas into your configurations and tests to keep mail flowing securely and predictably.
